Section: 3.1 Computational Theory of Mind and recursive actor models [1]
Claim: Recursive actor modeling is an established computational mechanism, not a PCC novelty claim. [1]
Supporting Sources: Interactive-POMDP and related frameworks treat recursive reasoning as integral to rational choice; empirical results observed mainly first- and second-level reasoning in human strategic tasks. [1]
Implication For Pcc: Cite ToM and bounded-recursion work; do not claim novelty for representing nested perspectives. [1]
Novelty Risk: High if PCC claims second-order belief representation as new. [1]

Section: 3.1 Computational Theory of Mind and recursive actor models [2] [3]
Claim: Actor-indexed attributions should be modeled as uncertain and bounded rather than as recovered private mental states. [2] [3]
Supporting Sources: Uncertain-ToM work identifies uncertainty from communication, interpretation, and trust, and adds probability estimates to formal agent-communication semantics. [2] Computational-ToM work argues that exhaustive tracking of individual mental attitudes is impractical and proposes abstractions. [3]
Implication For Pcc: Define apparent task commitments as revisable hypotheses supported by interactional evidence, not claims about inaccessible minds. [2] [3]
Novelty Risk: Medium; the framing is defensible if PCC remains explicit about public evidence and action-state use. [2] [3]

Section: 3.1 Computational Theory of Mind and recursive actor models [4]
Claim: Situated collaborative datasets can annotate beliefs about the world and about interaction partners. [4]
Supporting Sources: MindCraft records collaborative Minecraft tasks and captures partners’ beliefs of the world and of each other while interaction unfolds. [4]
Implication For Pcc: Benchmark design should distinguish actor-indexed attributed states from publicly grounded action state. [4]
Novelty Risk: High if PCC presents actor-indexed belief annotation as unprecedented. [4]

Section: 3.2 Mutual Theory of Mind, grounding, and common ground [5] [6]
Claim: Common ground is a coordination resource requiring ongoing update, while ToM and public grounding are related but distinct. [5] [6]
Supporting Sources: Clark and Brennan define common ground as mutual knowledge, beliefs, and assumptions that must be updated during collective action. [5] A computational grounding model treats grounding as dynamics in dialogue participants’ information states. [6]
Implication For Pcc: Treat private-state attribution and public warrant as separate variables; neither should be used as a proxy for the other. [5] [6]
Novelty Risk: Medium; conceptual distinction is useful but needs careful attribution rather than novelty language. [5] [6]

Section: 3.2 Mutual Theory of Mind, grounding, and common ground [7]
Claim: Grounding can be operationalized through shared accepted propositions, multimodal evidence, and update rules. [7]
Supporting Sources: Common Ground Tracking identifies task-relevant propositions accepted by all participants, predicts common-ground construction from multimodal interactions, and applies situated-evidence closure rules. [7]
Implication For Pcc: This is a primary near-equivalent comparator; distinguish PCC by operational state promotion, role/authority, and inspectable decision rationale. [7]

Section: 3.2 Mutual Theory of Mind, grounding, and common ground [8]
Claim: Repair is a structured response to interactional trouble, rather than evidence that grounding has been achieved. [8]
Supporting Sources: Other-initiated repair has an inductively grounded, cross-linguistic annotation scheme tested in 12 languages. [8]
Implication For Pcc: Position clarification and repair as possible controls after insufficient warrant is diagnosed. [8]
Novelty Risk: High if PCC claims to introduce repair-oriented ambiguity handling. [8]

Section: 3.3 Public commitment, warrant, and promotion into shared action state [9]
Claim: Public commitment and grounding have formal computational accounts. [9]
Supporting Sources: Asher and Lascarides define grounding through shared public commitments and connect them to private attitudes in dynamic logic. [9]
Implication For Pcc: Cite this lineage prominently; PCC cannot claim public commitment as a new construct. [9]

Section: 3.3 Public commitment, warrant, and promotion into shared action state [10]
Claim: Ambiguity can alter the evolution of common commitments in dialogue. [10]
Supporting Sources: Venant and Asher provide a dynamic commitment semantics for ambiguity and its effects on commitment evolution, including common commitments. [10]
Implication For Pcc: Avoid claiming novelty for ambiguity-conditioned commitment evolution; test whether PCC adds workplace action-state, authorization, and warrant diagnostics. [10]

Section: 3.3 Public commitment, warrant, and promotion into shared action state [11]
Claim: Situated dialogue models can update commitments and constrain subsequent action-relevant moves across modalities. [11]
Supporting Sources: Piwek’s model updates partner commitments, constrains possible dialogue moves, embeds communication in overall activity, and accommodates language, object manipulation, and gesture. [11]
Implication For Pcc: PCC must make its operational-promotion criterion and public-evidence trace more explicit than a commitment-update model. [11]

Section: 3.4 Action-sensitive ambiguity, clarification, and ask-versus-act decisions [12] [13]
Claim: Question choice and clarification have established value- and utility-sensitive formulations. [12] [13]
Supporting Sources: Rao and Daumé rank clarification questions using expected value of perfect information. [12] Gervits et al. use a decision network with entropy-based utility for multimodal reference resolution. [13]
Implication For Pcc: Do not frame action-sensitive ambiguity as a new concept; use this literature as baseline and motivation. [12] [13]

Section: 3.4 Action-sensitive ambiguity, clarification, and ask-versus-act decisions [14]
Claim: The choice to clarify can depend jointly on uncertainty and the costs of wrong action. [14]
Supporting Sources: Tsvilodub et al. formalize an expected-regret tradeoff and report that humans seek clarification in proportion to loss risk under uncertainty. [14]
Implication For Pcc: PCC must distinguish its public-warrant/shared-state target from an individual act-versus-clarify policy. [14]

Section: 3.5 Situated coordination in collaborative work [15]
Claim: Cooperative work blends flexible alignment with predefined workflow rather than reducing coordination to either alone. [15]
Supporting Sources: Schmidt and Simone contrast ad hoc alignment and improvisation with predefined workflow and argue that the modalities are blended in real work. [15]
Implication For Pcc: Model roles, policy, artifacts, and workflow state as context that informs warrant rather than as fixed substitutes for human coordination. [15]
Novelty Risk: Medium; PCC’s workplace focus is well motivated but not a new CSCW premise. [15]

Section: 3.5 Situated coordination in collaborative work [16]
Claim: Articulation work can remain invisible in process representations and changes under automation. [16]
Supporting Sources: Novak and Lorenzi define articulation work as enabling distributed coordination, note its invisibility in flowcharts, and examine its transformation under barcode medication administration. [16]
Implication For Pcc: Use inspection outputs to expose otherwise invisible coordination assumptions and state transitions. [16]
Novelty Risk: Low for applying the idea to PCC; high for claiming to discover articulation work. [16]

Section: 3.6 Observability, abstention, and contestability [17] [18]
Claim: Explainable collaboration requires reasoning over task and collaborator models, and uncertainty display alone may be insufficient for calibrated reliance. [17] [18]
Supporting Sources: Kambhampati links explainable collaborative behavior to reasoning over task and human mental models. [17] A pre-registered study found uncertainty displays alone did not improve team performance or user mental models, while capability-focused guidance improved correct self-reliance. [18]
Implication For Pcc: Evaluate whether evidence-plus-consequence displays improve diagnostic judgment and calibrated reliance, not merely whether they are shown. [17] [18]

Section: 3.6 Observability, abstention, and contestability [19]
Claim: Abstention can be paired with locally interpretable explanations of the decision to refrain. [19]
Supporting Sources: A selective-classification method uses counterfactual distance to support explanations of whether a decision should be issued or withheld. [19]
Implication For Pcc: Make abstention and request-for-clarification evidence-bearing outputs, not opaque non-actions. [19]

Section: 3.7 Synthesis: PCC between attributed state and shared action [9, 7, 14, 20]
Claim: PCC’s safest provisional contribution is a combination: public-evidence-based diagnostic control over promotion into a role- and artifact-governed shared action state. [9, 7, 14, 20]
Supporting Sources: The current corpus separately establishes public-commitment grounding, multimodal common-ground updates, action-cost-sensitive clarification, and evidence-gated tool calls. [9, 7, 14, 20]
Implication For Pcc: State this as an audit hypothesis until full-text review tests whether any prior system already combines the entire mechanism. [9, 7, 14, 20]
Novelty Risk: Medium–high until the closest full texts are audited. [9, 7, 14, 20]
